title: What Confucius Taught His Own Son
text:
Confucius had one son, Kong Li, known as Boyu. Since Confucius taught many disciples, some of them wondered whether he kept special teachings for his own family. The Analects record what happened when a man named Chen Kang put the question directly.

Chen Kang asked Boyu whether he had heard any lessons from his father different from what the other students heard. Boyu said no. Once, he said, his father was standing alone when Boyu hurried past through the courtyard. Confucius asked whether he had studied the Book of Odes. When Boyu said not yet, his father told him that without the Odes he would have nothing to say in conversation, so Boyu went and studied them. Another day, in the same way, Confucius asked whether he had studied the rites. When Boyu said not yet, his father told him that without the rites he would have no ground to stand on. So he studied the rites. Those two things, Boyu said, were all he had heard.

Chen Kang went away delighted. He had asked about one thing, he said, and learned three: about the Odes, about the rites, and that a gentleman keeps a certain distance from his own son.

Boyu died before his father. Elsewhere the Analects record that Confucius gave him a plain burial, as his means and position allowed.
lesson: Children deserve the same honest teaching as everyone else, not secret favors. Sometimes the most useful thing a parent does is ask a simple question at the right moment.
source: Confucius, Analects 16.13 and 11.8, trans. James Legge
